**Problem 1**

```{r}
data=read_excel("../../data/Chapter12_exercises_data.xls", sheet="Exercise 1-2")
y=as.numeric(data$GDP, na.omit=TRUE)
c=as.numeric(data$CONSUMPTION, na.omit=TRUE)
y=ts(y, start=c(1947,1), end=c(2012,4), freq=4)
c=ts(c, start=c(1947,1), end=c(2012,4), freq=4)
ly=log(y)
lc=log(c)

plot(ly, type="l", col="blue", ylab="Log GDP", xlab="Time", ylim=c(7, 10))
lines(lc, col="red")
adf.test(ly)
adf.test(lc)

adf.test(diff(ly))
adf.test(diff(lc))
```

The two time series are non-stationary which is a good requirement for cointegration. They are also economically correlated and share similar dynamics in the plot. Their differences are stationary, which is a good requirement for cointegration. 

```{r}
comodel=lm(lc~ly)
summary(comodel)

resid=residuals(comodel)
adf.test(resid)
```

After running the model, we can see that the R^2 is very high which is good for cointegration. However, the residuals are not stationary because the p-value (.051) is above 5%. Therefore, this is not a cointegrated relationship at the 5% level, although the result is borderline.

**Problem 2**

```{r}
ci=cbind(ly,lc)
jt=ca.jo(ci)
summary(jt)

tw=ly-.934*lc
adf.test(tw)

plot(tw)
```

The Johansen maximal eigenvalue test rejects r = 0 at the 5% level (17.77 > 14.90) but not at the 1% level, and does not reject r <= 1, which points to one cointegrating relationship. However, the adf test on the combination given by the first eigenvector (ly - .934lc) has a p-value of .055, so it is not stationary at the 5% level. Together with Problem 1, the evidence for a cointegrating relationship between GDP and consumption is borderline.

**Problem 3**


```{r}
data=read_excel("../../data/Chapter12_exercises_data.xls", sheet="Exercise 3")
cpigermany=ts(data$CPI_Germany, start=c(1999,1), end=c(2013,1), freq=12)
cpius=ts(data$CPI_US, start=c(1999,1), end=c(2013,1), freq=12)
ex=ts(data$EX_dollar_euro, start=c(1999,1), end=c(2013,1), freq=12)

wt=cpius-ex*cpigermany
adf.test(wt)
```

After running the adf test on the residuals of cpius-ex*cpigermany, we can see that the residuals are not stationary because the p-value is 35%. This means that there is not a cointegrated relationship and that the PPP does not hold.

**Problem 4**

```{r}
data=read_excel("../../data/Chapter12_exercises_data.xls", sheet="Exercise 7")
la=ts(data$ILA, start=c(1975,1), end=c(2012,4), freq=4)
rv=ts(data$IRV, start=c(1975,1), end=c(2012,4), freq=4)

ci=cbind(la,rv)
jt=ca.jo(ci)
summary(jt)

tw=la-1.4315*rv
adf.test(tw)

plot(tw)

plot(forecast(ets(tw), h=3), xlim=c(2000,2014))
```

Yes, from the adf test on the johansen test eigenvectors, we can see that they are stationary which means that there is a cointegrated relationship. We can see that the forecast shows that the series is going to mean revert to the long run equilibrium.

**Problem 5**

```{r}
set.seed(144)
spec=ugarchspec(
variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(4, 0)),
mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
distribution.model = "norm")
setfixed(spec) <- list(
  mu = 0,
  omega = 0.1,
  alpha1 = 0.20,
  alpha2 = 0.15,
  alpha3 = 0.10,
  alpha4 = 0.05
)

sim <- ugarchpath(spec, n.sim = 2000, n.start = 500, m.sim = 1)

mu  <- as.numeric(fitted(sim))
eps <- as.numeric(sim@path$seriesSim)
y   <- mu + eps

sig  <- as.numeric(sigma(sim))
sig2 <- sig^2
z   <- eps / sig

plot(y, type="l", main="Simulated ARCH(4) series")
plot(sig2, type="l", main="Conditional variance sigma_t^2")
par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4,4,2,1))
hist(y, breaks=40, main="Histogram: original series y_t", xlab="y_t")
hist(z, breaks=40, main="Histogram: standardized series z_t", xlab="z_t")

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
acf(y,    lag.max=40, ylab="ACF y_t")
acf(y^2,  lag.max=40, ylab="ACF y_t^2")
acf(z,    lag.max=40, ylab="ACF z_t")
acf(z^2,  lag.max=40, ylab="ACF z_t^2")
```

The standardized series follows a normal distribution better than the original series. The ACF of y_t^2 is relevant and shows that a GARCH model is appropriate. The non-squared ACFs are not relevant, which shows why squaring y_t is necessary.

**Problem 6**

```{r}
set.seed(144)
spec_low <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(model="sGARCH", garchOrder=c(1,1)),
  mean.model = list(armaOrder=c(0,0), include.mean=TRUE),
  distribution.model="norm"
)

setfixed(spec_low) <- list(
  mu = 0,
  omega = 0.1,
  alpha1 = 0.15,
  beta1  = 0.25
)

sim_low <- ugarchpath(spec_low, n.sim=2000, n.start=500)

y_low  <- as.numeric(fitted(sim_low)) + as.numeric(sim_low@path$seriesSim)
sig2_low <- as.numeric(sigma(sim_low))^2

z_low <- y_low / sqrt(sig2_low)

spec_high <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(model="sGARCH", garchOrder=c(1,1)),
  mean.model = list(armaOrder=c(0,0), include.mean=TRUE),
  distribution.model="norm"
)

setfixed(spec_high) <- list(
  mu = 0,
  omega = 0.1,
  alpha1 = 0.10,
  beta1  = 0.88
)

sim_high <- ugarchpath(spec_high, n.sim=2000, n.start=500)

y_high  <- as.numeric(fitted(sim_high)) + as.numeric(sim_high@path$seriesSim)
sig2_high <- as.numeric(sigma(sim_high))^2
z_high <- y_high / sqrt(sig2_high)

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(y_low, type="l", ylab="Low Volatility Series")
plot(y_high, type="l", ylab="High Volatility Series")

plot(sig2_low, type="l", ylab="Conditional variance sigma_t^2 (Low Volatility)")
plot(sig2_high, type="l", ylab="Conditional variance sigma_t^2 (High Volatility)")

hist(y_low, breaks=40, main="Histogram: original series y_low")
hist(y_high, breaks=40, main="Histogram: original series y_high")
hist(z_low, breaks=40, main="Histogram: standardized series z_low")
hist(z_high, breaks=40, main="Histogram: standardized series z_high")
acf(y_low,    lag.max=40, ylab="ACF y_low (Low Volatility)")
acf(y_high,    lag.max=40, ylab="ACF y_high (High Volatility)")
acf(z_low,    lag.max=40, ylab="ACF z_low (Low Volatility)")
acf(z_high,    lag.max=40, ylab="ACF z_high (High Volatility)")
acf(y_low^2,  lag.max=40, ylab="ACF y_low^2 (Low Volatility)")
acf(y_high^2,  lag.max=40, ylab="ACF y_high^2 (High Volatility)")
acf(z_low^2,  lag.max=40, ylab="ACF z_low^2 (Low Volatility)")
acf(z_high^2,  lag.max=40, ylab="ACF z_high^2 (High Volatility)")
```

The two histograms are similar, however, the standardized series follows a normal distribution better than the original series. The ACF of the Yt^2 shows that there are volatility dynamics in the series and that a garch model is appropriate. This cannot be seen in the non-squared ACFs.

**Problem 7**

```{r}
model=ugarchspec(
variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(2, 2)),
mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(2, 2), include.mean = TRUE),
distribution.model = "norm")
getSymbols("^GSPC", src = "yahoo", from = "2000-01-01", to = "2025-12-31")
sp500 <- na.omit(Ad(GSPC))
sp500_old <- sp500["2000-01-01/2010-12-31"]
sp500_new <- sp500["2015-01-01/2025-12-31"]
sp500old <- ts(as.numeric(sp500_old), 
               start = c(2000, 1), 
               frequency = 252)
sp500new <- ts(as.numeric(sp500_new), 
               start = c(2015, 1), 
               frequency = 252)
head(sp500old)
head(sp500new)

returns_old=diff(log(sp500old))*100
returns_new=diff(log(sp500new))*100

par(mfrow=c(2,1))
plot(returns_old, main="S&P 500 Old Returns")
plot(returns_new, main="S&P 500 New Returns")

tsdisplay(returns_old)
tsdisplay(returns_new)

tsdisplay(returns_old^2)
tsdisplay(returns_new^2)

modelfit=ugarchfit(spec=model,data=returns_new)
modelfit
```

Returns from 2000-2010 has higher volatility in returns compared to returns from 2015-2025. There are definitely times of high and low volatility throughout both periods.

The model after the PACF of the Y^2 looks like it could be a very high order ARCH model. After running ugarch, a garch(2,2) can also be used in conjunction with an arma(2,2) model.

**Problem 8**

```{r}
modelfor = ugarchforecast(modelfit, data = NULL, n.ahead = 2, n.roll =0 , out.sample = 0)
modelfor
plot(modelfor, which=1)
```
